source.title: Architecture, Not Scale: Circuit Localization in Large Language Models

page_placements.theme: Redundancy and shifting identity of induction heads; distribution depends on architecture

record.tranche_reason: The study measures induction-related behavior in pretrained models using repeated-token sequences, attention scores, and greedy ablations, rather than reproducing the original training-time measurements.
record.gate_note: The study tests induction behavior on synthetic repeated-token sequences. It does not measure training-time formation, loss-curve bumps, or induction-head composition with a previous-token head. Its IOI and factual-recall results do not bear on the claim versions about induction heads.
record.test_reason: The study measures induction behaviour (ICL advantage, attention at the induction offset, greedy-ablation damage) in six pretrained Pythia and Qwen2.5 models from 160M to 7B. This bears on V4, whether induction heads appear across families and sizes. It does not track training, so V2, V5 and V7 are not tested. It does not test previous-token composition (V1) or the share of ICL carried by these heads (V3, V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that attention architecture (GQA vs MHA), not scale, determines how concentrated circuits are, for IOI, induction and factual recall alike. Qwen2.5 induction breaks after 2 to 6 ablations, while Pythia's induction circuit is distributed and grows more so with scale. Pythia-160M shows no functional induction circuit. They acknowledge that architecture is confounded with training data, tokenizer and recipe.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained Pythia and Qwen2.5 models and synthetic repeated-token sequences, measuring attention at the induction offset and greedy-ablation damage; it does not reproduce the original training-time formation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Induction-circuit concentration differs between the Pythia MHA and Qwen2.5 GQA model families; Pythia-160M lacks measurable functional induction behavior while the larger tested models show positive ICL advantage.

fits_no_version.finding: Induction-circuit concentration differs by attention architecture. GQA Qwen2.5 models break after 2 to 6 ablations, while MHA Pythia models need 22 to 28, and Pythia becomes more distributed with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How many heads carry induction behaviour depends on the attention architecture (GQA vs MHA) more than on model size.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The study tests a small number of models from two families and does not control for differences in training data, tokenizer, or training recipe, which the authors acknowledge confound the architectural comparison.
record.rows_left_out: IOI and factual-recall results were omitted because they do not measure induction behavior. Figure 6 heatmap descriptions were not added as separate rows because the table reports per-model induction metrics and the figure provides qualitative score distributions without separate numerical values.

untested.parts: Composition with a previous-token head and small attention-only models are not tested. The two-head mechanism is only described in the background section.
No training trajectory, phase change or loss bump is measured.
Whether induction heads carry most in-context learning on natural text is not measured.
Multiple training runs, other architectures beyond MHA/GQA transformers, and other modalities are not tested.
Data and training setup are not varied. The authors say architecture is confounded with data, tokenizer and recipe.
Few-shot task learning is not compared with copying.
Formation over training is not tracked.

missing.what: Attention-based induction scores per head (mean attention at the induction offset). Pythia-160M has one dominant cell at layer 8, and the number of high-scoring heads grows with scale in Pythia. Qwen2.5 scores sit in mid-to-late layer bands (layers 14-20 for 1.5B). This is qualitative only, and it conflicts with the claim that 160M has no induction circuit.
The top-scoring ICL head differs from the top IOI head in all six models.

record.verdict_notes: I removed the reader's V4 limits_scope label about covering only two families; that is untested scope, not a qualifying result. Pythia-160M's negative ICL advantage (loss worse than chance) is surprising, and Figure 6 conflicts with it, so treat it cautiously. No uncertainty estimates or seeds are reported. The IOI and factual-recall rows are rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the proposed composition with a previous-token head, nor does it test small attention-only transformers.
No training-time trajectory, abrupt formation window, loss bump, or timing relationship between formation and in-context learning is measured.
The study tests a synthetic repeated-token task, not whether induction heads carry most in-context learning in large transformers.
It tests induction behavior in six models from two architecture families and several sizes, but not multiple training runs, other architectures beyond those families, or other modalities.
Training data and setup are not varied independently. The authors note that architecture is confounded with training data, tokenizer, and recipe.
The study does not compare induction heads with other mechanisms for few-shot task learning.
The study does not track formation over training or resolve separate formation sub-steps.

relationships.condition: Pythia-1.4B, Pythia-6.9B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/7B on random repeated-token sequences
relationships.reason: ICL advantage is positive at +5.6 to +7.4 (r4, r7, r10, r13, r16). Ablating heads destroys the in-context prediction (r5, r6, r8, r9, r11, r12, r14, r15, r17, r18), across two families and 0.5B to 7B.
relationships.display_finding: In-context learning advantage ranges from +5.6 to +7.4, and head ablation destroys in-context prediction across the tested 0.5B–7B models.

relationships.reason: ICL advantage is negative at −7.668 (r1) and ablating more than 20 heads does no meaningful damage (r3), so no functional induction circuit appears at this size. Caveat: Figure 6 shows a dominant L8 attention cell, so the result may depend on the measure.
relationships.display_finding: In-context learning advantage is −7.668, and ablating more than 20 heads causes no meaningful damage, despite a dominant layer-8 attention cell.
